se.name: Sé Cathedral
se.why: Romanesque-turned-Baroque cathedral, with views over the Ribeira rooftops.
se.story:
Porto's cathedral began as a **Romanesque fortress-church** in the 12th century, its thick walls built as much for defence as for worship. Later additions layered on Gothic cloisters and a Baroque facelift, so what you're looking at is really eight centuries stacked on top of each other. The terrace out front gives one of the best free views over the Ribeira rooftops.

[Read more on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto_Cathedral)

sao-lourenco.name: Igreja de São Lourenço / MASA
sao-lourenco.why: Church plus a modern art museum in one visit.
sao-lourenco.story:
Locals call it *Igreja dos Grilos* — "Church of the Crickets" — after the Augustinian friars nicknamed "Crickets" who once lived here. Built by Jesuits in the 16th century, it now shares its home with the **MASA** museum of sacred art and archaeology next door.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igreja_dos_Grilos)

mirador-sao-lourenco.name: Miradouro da Igreja de São Lourenço
mirador-sao-lourenco.why: Quick free viewpoint right by São Lourenço.
mirador-sao-lourenco.story: A small, easy-to-miss viewpoint that opens up right beside São Lourenço — no ticket, no queue, just rooftops and river.

mirador-vitoria.name: Miradouro da Vitória
mirador-vitoria.why: One of the best classic postcard views over the rooftops and river.
mirador-vitoria.story: One of Porto's classic postcard shots: terracotta roofs tumbling down to the Douro, with Vila Nova de Gaia's wine lodges on the far bank. Best in late afternoon light.

mirador-virtudes.name: Miradouro das Virtudes
mirador-virtudes.why: Terraced garden viewpoint, great for a breather.
mirador-virtudes.story: A terraced garden that locals treat as a living room — benches, a view toward the *Ponte da Arrábida*, and a lively bar scene at sunset.

sao-bento.name: São Bento Station
sao-bento.why: Working station; its azulejo panels depict Portuguese history, not just scenery.
sao-bento.story:
Still a working train station, but the real destination is the entrance hall: roughly **20,000 azulejo tiles** painted between 1905 and 1916, depicting historical battles and the arrival of the railway itself. It sits on the site of a former Benedictine monastery, which is where the station gets its name.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Bento_railway_station)

trindade.name: Igreja da Santíssima Trindade
trindade.why: One of Porto's largest churches, free to step into.
trindade.story: A 19th-century neoclassical church behind the city hall, built to a design by **Carlos Amarante** — who's buried inside it. Quietly grand rather than showy, and usually free of the crowds a few streets over.

camara.name: Câmara Municipal do Porto
camara.why: Porto's city hall — worth a look from the outside.
camara.story: Porto's city hall, dating back administratively to **1614**, though the current granite building is 20th-century. Worth a glance from Avenida dos Aliados even if you don't go in — it anchors one end of the city's grandest avenue.

bolhao.name: Mercado do Bolhão
bolhao.why: Restored historic market — good for snacks and people-watching.
bolhao.story: A restored neoclassical market hall on two levels, mostly fishmongers, butchers, and flower stalls rather than tourist stands — go for the atmosphere, stay for a coffee at one of the counters.

almas.name: Capela das Almas
almas.why: A chapel entirely covered in blue azulejo tiles.
almas.story:
Technically the *Chapel of Santa Catarina*, but everyone calls it Capela das Almas — "Chapel of Souls." Its exterior is wrapped in nearly **16,000 azulejo tiles**, added in 1929, depicting scenes from the lives of St. Francis and St. Catherine.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_Santa_Catarina)

ildefonso.name: Igreja de Santo Ildefonso
ildefonso.story:
An 18th-century church whose azulejo facade — about **11,000 tiles**, added in 1932 — was designed by the same artist, Jorge Colaço, who tiled São Bento station.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Saint_Ildefonso)

carmo.name: Igreja do Carmo + square
carmo.why: Twin-church complex with an equally famous tiled side wall.
carmo.story: A Baroque/Rococo church covered in tiles added in 1912. Look for the **Casa Escondida** next door — a house barely a metre wide, built, legend says, so the neighbouring Carmo and Carmelitas churches wouldn't have to share a wall.

lello.name: Livraria Lello
lello.why: World-famous bookshop — book a timed entry slot ahead.
lello.story:
One of the world's most photographed bookshops, known for its carved wooden staircase and stained-glass ceiling. The Harry Potter connection gets overstated — J.K. Rowling lived in Porto and may have visited, but the "inspiration" story is more myth than confirmed fact. Worth going anyway, purely on its own merits.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livraria_Lello)

clerigos.name: Torre dos Clérigos + Museum
clerigos.why: Climb the tower for the best panoramic view of the city.
clerigos.story:
At 75 metres, this was the **tallest building in Portugal** when it was finished in 1763. Its architect, **Nicolau Nasoni**, liked the church so much he asked to be buried in its crypt — the exact spot is still unknown. Climb the 240-odd steps for the best panoramic view in the city.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%C3%A9rigos_Church)

sao-francisco.name: Igreja e Museu de São Francisco
sao-francisco.why: Gothic church with an extraordinarily ornate gilded interior.
sao-francisco.story:
Gothic on the outside, almost absurdly ornate on the inside — an estimated **100 kilograms of gold leaf** covers the Baroque woodcarving. Part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_S%C3%A3o_Francisco_(Porto))

ribeira.name: Cais da Ribeira
ribeira.why: The classic riverside strip — colourful houses, cafés, river views.
ribeira.story: The riverfront that's been Porto's working waterfront since the Middle Ages — and, since 1996, part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. Colourful houses, cafés, and the best angle on the Dom Luís I bridge.

elevador.name: Elevador da Ribeira
elevador.why: Funicular shortcut up from the riverside to the upper town.
elevador.story: A small funicular that saves you the climb from the riverside up to the Batalha area — quick, cheap, and a nice break for tired legs partway through the day.

serralves.name: Serralves
serralves.why: Art deco villa, park, contemporary art museum and Treetop Walk.
serralves.story: An Art Deco villa turned into one of Portugal's leading contemporary art museums, set in a landscaped park with a treetop walkway. Come for the art, stay for the gardens.

banco-materiais.name: Banco de Materiais
banco-materiais.why: Small, free museum of architectural materials and tiles.
banco-materiais.story: A small, free museum of architectural materials — tiles, stonework, fittings — salvaged from buildings around the city. Niche, but a nice quiet stop between bigger sights.

bolsa.name: Palácio da Bolsa
bolsa.why: Former stock exchange — the Arabian Room was built to impress a visiting king, not from Islamic-era Porto.
bolsa.story:
Porto's former stock exchange, built after an 1832 fire destroyed the São Francisco monastery's cloister. The showstopper is the **Salão Árabe** — the Arab Room — a gilded, Moorish-style hall built in the 1860s to impress a visiting king, not a genuine relic of Islamic-era Porto. Guided tour only.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pal%C3%A1cio_da_Bolsa)

ponte.name: Ponte Dom Luís I
ponte.why: Iconic double-deck iron bridge — walk both levels for different views.
ponte.story:
A double-deck iron bridge completed in **1886** by **Théophile Seyrig**, who trained under Gustave Eiffel's firm. The lower deck carries traffic and pedestrians at river level; the upper deck, now used by the metro, gives the best view in the city.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom_Lu%C3%ADs_I_Bridge)

cais-gaia.name: Cais de Gaia
cais-gaia.why: Riverside promenade on the Gaia side, facing the Ribeira.
cais-gaia.story: The Gaia-side mirror of the Ribeira — same river, same postcard views, fewer crowds, and it's where all the port wine cellars actually are.

coelho.name: O Coelho — Bordalo II
coelho.why: Giant recycled-material rabbit street art installation.
coelho.story: A giant rabbit built entirely from recycled trash and scrap metal by Portuguese street artist **Bordalo II**, part of his "Big Trash Animals" series highlighting waste and pollution.

winery.name: Wine cellar — e.g. Caves Cálem
winery.why: Port wine cellar tour + tasting — book a slot in advance.
winery.story: Port wine can only legally be aged and shipped from Vila Nova de Gaia, a quirk of 18th-century trade rules — which is why every major port house (Cálem, Graham's, Taylor's) has its cellars on this side of the river, not in Porto proper.

teleferico.name: Teleférico de Gaia
teleferico.why: Cable car over the Gaia riverside with wide Douro views.
teleferico.story: A cable car running along the Gaia riverside, giving a bird's-eye view of the port wine cellars and both bridges without the climb.

serra-pilar.name: Serra do Pilar + viewpoint
serra-pilar.why: Best sunset viewpoint over both riverbanks — monastery closed, but the 1832–33 siege was fought right here.
serra-pilar.story: A 16th-century monastery with a circular cloister, perched on the hill above Gaia. It played a real military role in the **1832–33 Siege of Porto**, and the viewpoint beside it is one of the best sunset spots in the city — the monastery interior itself is currently closed.

palacio-cristal.name: Jardins do Palácio de Cristal
palacio-cristal.why: Sweeping garden terraces with river and city views, peacocks included.
palacio-cristal.story:
Named for a 19th-century iron-and-glass exhibition hall that was demolished in 1951 and replaced by a sports arena — the gardens around it outlived the building itself. Eight hectares of terraces, ponds, and some of the best river views in the city.

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_(Porto))

sentimentos.name: Jardim dos Sentimentos
sentimentos.why: A quiet, less-visited corner within the same gardens.
sentimentos.story: A quieter corner of the same Crystal Palace gardens — same river views, far fewer people.

history.title: A very short history of Porto
history.subtitle: Nine moments that explain what you're walking through

portus-cale.title: Portus Cale
portus-cale.note: Roman twin settlements on the Douro give **Portugal** its name. [More →](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portus_Cale)

county.title: County of Portugal
county.note: Founded here in **1096** — where the nation began.

ceuta-fleet.title: Henry the Navigator's fleet
ceuta-fleet.note: Porto sent its meat to the ships, kept the tripe — hence *"tripeiros."*

methuen.title: Treaty of Methuen
methuen.note: Cements the England–Portugal wine trade — why it's called **"Port."** [More →](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methuen_Treaty)

ponte-barcas.title: Ponte das Barcas disaster
ponte-barcas.note: A pontoon bridge collapse during the Peninsular War, ~4,000 dead. [More →](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto_Boat_Bridge_disaster)

ponte-dom-luis.title: Ponte Dom Luís I completed
ponte-dom-luis.note: By **Théophile Seyrig**, of Gustave Eiffel's firm.

capital-of-culture.title: European Capital of Culture
capital-of-culture.note: Porto's year in the spotlight — it's also how the city got **Casa da Música**.

surfing.title: Surfing 101: catch a wave
surfing.subtitle: The basics, in case Porto's beaches tempt you

paddle.title: Paddle
paddle.description: Lie flat, paddle to match the wave's speed.

pop-up.title: Pop up
pop-up.description: One motion: hands push, feet land — front foot forward, knees bent.

stance.title: Stance
stance.description: Weight centred, eyes up, arms out for balance.

ride.title: Ride
ride.description: Steer by shifting your weight; kick out before it closes.

tips.wetsuit: Wear a wetsuit — the Atlantic stays ~18°C even in September.
tips.board: Start on a foam board — softer, more forgiving, easier to pop up on.
tips.etiquette: One wave, one surfer — don't drop in on someone already riding.
tips.leash: Always use a leash — a loose board is a hazard to everyone nearby.
tips.conditions: Check conditions and rip currents before paddling out.
tips.lesson: A first lesson beats a day of guessing — local schools rent gear too.

spot.title: Nearest surf beach: Matosinhos
spot.description: ~20 min from the centre by metro (Line A to Mercado). Consistent beach break, several schools for beginners.

francesinha.title: Francesinha
francesinha.story: Bread, ham, sausage, and steak stacked and drenched in a spicy tomato-beer sauce, then blanketed in melted cheese with a fried egg on top. Invented in Porto in the 1950s as a local twist on the French *croque-monsieur* — **francesinha** literally means "little French girl."

tripas.title: Tripas à moda do Porto
tripas.story: Porto's people are nicknamed **tripeiros** — "tripe eaters" — after a local legend: in 1415, the city sent all its meat to provision Henry the Navigator's fleet for the conquest of Ceuta, keeping only the offal for themselves. The dish became a point of pride rather than an insult.

bacalhau-gomes-de-sa.title: Bacalhau à Gomes de Sá
bacalhau-gomes-de-sa.story: One of hundreds of ways Portugal cooks salt cod — this one layers it with potatoes, onions, olives, and hard-boiled egg. Said to be invented by a Porto merchant, Gomes de Sá, sometime in the 19th century.

bifana.title: Bifana
bifana.story: A thin pork cutlet, marinated and pan-fried, stuffed into a plain bread roll — sometimes with nothing more than a smear of mustard. Cheap, fast, and everywhere.

caldo-verde.title: Caldo verde
caldo-verde.story: Shredded kale in a potato broth, usually finished with a slice of smoky *chouriço* and a drizzle of olive oil. Northern Portugal's answer to comfort food.

pastel-de-nata.title: Pastéis de nata
pastel-de-nata.story: Custard tart with a caramelised top and impossibly flaky pastry — technically a Lisbon invention, but you'll find a version on nearly every Porto counter, and no trip is complete without one.

vinho-do-porto.title: Port wine
vinho-do-porto.note: Tawny, ruby, or white — try all three in Gaia
vinho-do-porto.story: A fortified wine that, by law, can only carry the name "Port" if it's aged in Vila Nova de Gaia. **Tawny** ages in wood and turns nutty and amber; **ruby** stays fruity and red; **white** is the rarer, lighter option worth asking for.

vinho-verde.title: Vinho Verde
vinho-verde.story: "Green wine" — not the colour, but the age: bottled young, drunk young, with a light natural fizz. From the Minho region just north of Porto, and usually cheaper than the water.

super-bock.title: Super Bock
super-bock.note: The local beer, rival to Sagres
super-bock.story: Porto's home beer, brewed since 1927, and the traditional rival to Lisbon-associated **Sagres** — order the "wrong" one in the wrong bar and you'll get a look.

bica.title: Bica
bica.note: Espresso, drunk standing at the counter
bica.story: Portuguese for a short, strong espresso — order it standing at the counter, the way most locals actually drink their coffee.

tripeiro.title: Tripeiro/a
tripeiro.story: *See the tripe story above* — this is simply what a Porto local calls themselves, with real pride, not embarrassment.

obrigadinho.title: Obrigadinho
obrigadinho.story: A softened, more casual version of *obrigado* ("thank you") — the diminutive "-inho" ending is a very Portuguese way of making something warmer, smaller, friendlier.

esta-bom.title: Está bom?
esta-bom.note: "Is it good?" — ask after a bite
esta-bom.story: Literally "is it good?" — the question you'll get asked, sincerely, after your first bite of almost anything.

cruzeiro-seis-pontes.title: 6-bridges Douro cruise
cruzeiro-seis-pontes.story: A boat trip along the Douro passing under all six of the bridges that connect Porto to Gaia, including the Dom Luís I — a different, lower angle on a city you've mostly been seeing from above.

perder-se-ribeira.title: Get lost in Ribeira
perder-se-ribeira.story: The Ribeira's medieval street plan wasn't built for efficiency — climbing staircases and narrow alleys on purpose, with no destination in mind, is arguably the best way to see it.

lello-cedo.title: Livraria Lello, early
lello-cedo.story: Livraria Lello gets genuinely crowded by mid-morning — arriving at opening time is the difference between a quiet browse and a queue around the block.

cachecol.title: Buy a scarf before the match
cachecol.story: Team scarves are sold outside Estádio do Dragão on match days — a cheap, practical souvenir that also happens to be useful in the stadium crowd.

o-classico.title: O Clássico
o-classico.note: Porto vs. Benfica — the rivalry that matters
o-classico.story: *O Clássico* is the FC Porto–Benfica fixture specifically — Portugal's biggest football rivalry, sharpened by a third rival, Sporting CP, in what's usually called the country's "Big Three."

dragoes.title: "Dragões"
dragoes.note: Porto's nickname, from the club crest
dragoes.story: FC Porto's nickname comes straight off their club crest, adopted in 1922: a green dragon curled beneath a crown.

cores-estadio.title: Wear blue and white
cores-estadio.story: Blue and white are FC Porto's colours — wear them without hesitation. **Red** belongs to Benfica, and wearing it near Estádio do Dragão on match day is a genuinely bad idea, not just a faux pas.

fado.title: Fado
fado.story: A genre built around **saudade** — a specifically Portuguese kind of longing that doesn't translate cleanly into English. Traditionally sung solo, accompanied by the pear-shaped Portuguese guitar, and more associated with Lisbon than Porto, though you'll still find fado houses here.

amalia-rodrigues.title: Amália Rodrigues
amalia-rodrigues.story: If one name defines fado, it's hers — a singer so central to the genre's 20th-century identity that Portugal declared three days of national mourning when she died in 1999.

vira-fandango.title: Vira / fandango
vira-fandango.note: Real folk dance, but rare to stumble into
vira-fandango.story: The *vira* is a real northern-Portuguese folk dance — quick, triple-time, danced face-to-face in a circle — but it lives in festivals and folk troupes now, not something you'll likely stumble into on a random Saturday night.

guide.subtitle: Practical basics for getting around Porto

rules-of-thumb.title: Trip rules of thumb
items: Friday is the most walking-heavy day — comfortable shoes.
Saturday starts slow on purpose (10:00–12:00 at Serralves).
Clérigos Tower is Saturday, not rushed into Friday.
Sunday flows straight into the match — no separate outing.
No beaches or Matosinhos on this trip.
Serra do Pilar: viewpoint only, monastery closed.
Rain backup: swap outdoor viewpoints for Bolsa, São Francisco, or Serralves' museum.

money.title: Currency & paying
items: Euro (€).
Cards/contactless widely accepted.
Small cafés/markets may want cash — carry coins.
Attractions are cheap (€3–€15) — exact change helps.

tipping.title: Tipping
items: Not obligatory.
Round up, or ~5–10% at a sit-down dinner.
Skip it for coffee/counter service.

getting-around.title: Getting around
items: Mostly on foot — comfortable shoes over transit passes.
Metro/tram/bus uses the Andante card, sold at stations.
Taxi/Uber for the post-match return.

essentials.title: In case of emergency
items: Emergency number: 112 (police, ambulance, fire).
Pharmacies (farmácia) are marked with a green cross.
If your phone dies: apartment address and flight time are on this page — worth a mental note or screenshot.
No signal? Once you've opened this app online, everything — itinerary, spots, photos — keeps working offline.
